finding: A worthwhile distinct article is supported: farmer as an occupational word versus Chasa identification; a precisely located western village showing unequal landholding and changing revenue office; shared agricultural ritual rather than exclusive caste custom. Sources do not support one creation date or founder, an exhaustive modern branch map, or automatic equivalence with Khandayat.

sources.title: Odisha District Gazetteers: Bhadrak
sources.publisher: Gopabandhu Academy of Administration, General Administration Department, Government of Odisha; Chief Editor Dr Taradatt
sources.locator: Printed40/PDF56, heading Chasa; frontmatter iii–iv/PDF6–7 compilation process.
sources.date_status: Frontmatter records work initiated May2015 and final discussions February–April2016. Exact edition/publication date not established; URL2023 upload is not publication date.
sources.claims: The gazetteer explains Chasa as farmer but explicitly distinguishes the occupation from caste identification: not every cultivator reports Chasa as caste. Use this direct distinction rather than inferring a Sanskrit etymology. Its very brief entry does not provide community founding history.
sources.strength: Original institutional district account; adequate lexical/social distinction, not linguistic etymology study.
limits: Do not adopt its unsupported suggestion of population majority as a measured statistic.
No Odia-script label or Chasha alternate verified here.
Adjacent Dagara or Gauda accounts are different communities, not Chasa branch evidence.

sources.title: M. Ahmed, A Monograph on Village Penthabahal (In Rairakhol Subdivision, District Sambalpur)
sources.publication: Census of India1961, VolumeXII, PartVI No1, Village Survey Series1; preface signed1July1962. Investigator Banamali Misra, tabulation officer N.C.Nayak.
sources.locator: Preface PDF12; printed5/PDF20 settlement;9/PDF24 households/subgroups;18/PDF37 grain storage;23/PDF42 land;31–32/PDF50–51 revenue reforms.
sources.claims: The survey counted15Chasa households and67people among37households/165people. It calls Bisi and Sahu local subgroups, and identifies headman Mukund Bisi. Twelve Chasa households owned land and held nearly87% of cultivated area; other communities also owned land. Rain-fed farming distinguished Bahal/Mal wetland from Aat upland. Grain receptacles called pudugs used stout straw ropes. The account dates abolition of Gountiahi revenue intermediation to1June1961, describes service-linked Bhogra land settlement and some transfer to Grama Sabha. Thus cultivation, land ownership and revenue office were different relationships, not an inherent quality of caste.
sources.strength: Original census village investigation with named personnel and tables; useful historical snapshot, not current survey.
limits: Exact fieldwork days not stated; use1961Census village study with1962preface, not invented survey date.
Bisi/Sahu are described locally; not an exhaustive Odisha branch classification.
Settlement narrative onpp4–5 has speculative dates and unsubstantiated comparative praise; if used, explicitly label reported village history, not proven migration chronology.
Some prose stereotypes bodies/intelligence/development; reject these, use measured observations cautiously.
Do not describe1961tenure changes as legal advice/current law.

sources.title: Bhabagrahi Misra, Rice Rituals of Orissa
sources.inspection: Full original12page PDF text inspected through web; journal bibliographic record inspected.
sources.locator: p236 scope/cultivation;pp238–240 Akshaya Trutiya seed baskets and two variants;pp240–241 transplantation;243 harvest/new rice.
sources.claims: Misra explicitly says land is cultivated by people of all castes and limits his study to plains rice rituals. He describes seed baskets and implements prepared for Akshaya Trutiya, and gives two different sowing accounts rather than one fixed ceremony. At transplantation he records an arum plant interpreted as Lakshmi by priests and associated with sheltering frogs/protecting seedlings in popular explanation. These are shared agrarian traditions in a1966study, not Chasa-only customs or instructions every family follows. Work, seasonal uncertainty and reverence are connected in this record.
sources.strength: Original scholarly folklore article; useful recorded practice and multiple interpretations.
limits: Reject opening Aryan/non-Aryan racial origin synthesis; not reliable caste genealogy.
No precisely named villages or fieldwork dates for each ritual; avoid claiming statewide uniformity or unchanged present practice.
Do not reproduce song lyrics; paraphrase practice only.
Report author-recorded ecological belief as belief, not proven agronomic mechanism.

sources.title: Akio Tanabe, Genealogies of the ‘Paika Rebellion’: Heterogeneities and Linkages
sources.publication: International Journal of Asian Studies17(1),2020,pp1–18; DOI10.1017/S1479591420000157
sources.locator: Paragraphs on Puri district census1891–1931 and changing identification, original HTML lines591–592; prior Paika/Khandayat inspected source.
sources.claims: The paper interprets changes in Puri district Chasa/Khandayat census labels as evidence of historically changing identification and status claims. Use only a short bridge to the Khandayat article, avoiding repetition of its numerical narrative. A historical overlap does not make all Chasas and Khandayats interchangeable.
sources.strength: Peer-reviewed historical anthropology, reused inspected source.
limits: District/period-specific interpretation; no universal present equivalence.
This should not dominate the Chasa article; its distinctive evidence is Penthabahal and agricultural practice.

narrative_plan.point: Concise historical identification caveat and crosslink to Khandayat, no repeated census-number block.

narrative_plan.section: One village, different relationships to land
narrative_plan.point: Place/time,15households, unequal land distribution, localBisi/Sahu and headman/service-land distinction. Choose facts to keep source-derived article+notes under200.
Shared plains ritual heritage: seed basket/first sowing and alternate interpretations of arum at transplantation. Avoid giving exclusive caste ownership or universal formula.

narrative_plan.section: What an origin account still needs
narrative_plan.point: No founder proven; future locality-specific family records and oral accounts needed. Heritage includes concrete work and named places without pretending one village describes all Odisha.
